params.textField: Medicines come in a wide assortment of formulations to ensure the optimal effects of the drug. For instance, if the medication needs to dissolve in the small intestine instead of the stomach, it may be *enteric-coated (EC)*. Those medications must not be chewed, because when it is broken up, the drug is exposed to the area that needed to be avoided. If a medication needs to be released over a long period of time, it can be made into a *sustained-release* but *controlled release* preparations release the medication more consistently. None of the medication preparations just discussed will avoid the hepatic first pass. But a *topical gel* which contains alcohol, or *topical ointment*, which contains fat soluble substances can permeate the skin and avoid the hepatic first pass. Meanwhile, *topical creams* are water-based preparations, so very little to none of the components will go systemic.

params.textField: It is important that you use the correct and accepted abbreviations so that others will understand the meaning. If a medication is to be taken orally, it is abbreviated as *PO*. All of those medications, regardless of the formulation, will go through the liver before getting to systemic circulation. So if a medication is highly metabolised into an inactive substance in the liver, and/or is difficult to absorb, another mode of administration, like Intramuscular injections (abbreviated as *IM*) or intravenous (abbreviated as *IV*) can be used. Twice daily is abbreviated as *bd*, three times daily is *tds* and four times daily is *qid*
